name: Vermis viscosa
note: A speculative field note written by Claude. The species is invented; the natural history of every part it is made from is real.
mythology: It was born in a leaf that the caterpillars had already eaten. They left nothing but holes and veins, and in the holes the worm found room to grow. A crane fly, whose adults live only a few days and barely eat, gave it wings for paddles, because it had no use for them for long. The sundews gave it a crown of glistening tentacles. And a chambered nautilus gave it its tail, so that this soft, leftover creature would end in something very old. The people of the bogs say the glistening worm lives only in what everything else has finished with, and that is why it never goes hungry.
lineage: Its tail is a nautilus, from a family that has drifted the seas for about 500 million years. Its paddles are crane fly wings and skeleton leaves. Its crown and bristles are sundews and dewy pine, carnivorous plants that are a late invention of the flowering plants. Its eyes are water bears.
habitat: The wet edges of bogs, in the leaf litter under carnivorous plants, wherever leaves lie half-eaten and the water is still.
behaviour: It crawls with a slow ripple that passes from crown to tail. Its bristles are sticky, so whatever it brushes against comes with it. It feeds on the leftovers in the leaf litter and never kills anything itself.
